name: c-trap
description: A curved RF-only linear trap: four rods bent around an arc, holding ions in a gas until they are pulsed out sideways. It is the injector of an orbital analyser, and the curvature is the point - ions ejected radially from a curved trap converge as they fly, so the packet arrives at the analyser spatially focused rather than as a line. A straight trap ejects a line and would need a lens to do the same job. This is the first device here whose geometry is neither a translational cross-section nor a surface of revolution: a curved axis is invariant under nothing, so it needs a genuine volume solve. The rods are chains of overlapping spheres along their centrelines, because a cylinder in this format is axis-aligned and a curved rod is not - which needed no new primitive, since `repeat` binds an index and cosPi/sinPi can place a bead anywhere. Overlapping copies at one potential are deliberate rather than tolerated; the overlap check refuses only conductors that disagree about what they hold. Adjacent rods are at opposite RF phase, as in any quadrupole: the in-plane pair (inner and outer) against the out-of-plane pair (top and bottom). They are exact negatives, so four rods reduce to one basis solve however many beads each is built from.

bendRadius.description: Radius of the arc the trap axis follows. Smaller bends focus an ejected packet harder and are harder to build; this is the number the whole device exists to have.

arcHalfTurns.description: How far round the arc goes, in half turns - 0.5 is a quarter circle, which is the usual shape. Half turns rather than radians for the reason the multipole guide uses them: cosPi(0.5) is exactly zero where Math.Cos(pi/2) is 6.1e-17, and a rod placed a hair off axis puts a spurious dipole made of rounding into a device whose whole job is not to have one.

inscribedRadius.description: Axis to nearest rod surface, conventionally r0. The Mathieu q goes as its square at fixed voltage, so it is the length the working point is most sensitive to.

rodRatio.description: Rod radius as a multiple of the inscribed radius. Denison's value, which cancels the leading non-ideal multipole for STRAIGHT round rods - what it does for bent ones is a question this template exists to make askable.

beadCount.description: Beads per rod. They must overlap or the rod is a string of pearls with gaps the field reaches through: the spacing is the arc length over beadCount - 1, and it wants to be comfortably under the rod radius. Raising it costs solve time and buys smoothness, and the field between beads is the thing to check when it looks wrong.

rfAmplitude.description: Zero to peak on the in-plane pair; the out-of-plane pair takes its exact negative, which is what makes the four rods one basis solve.

driveFrequency.description: One generator for the whole structure. A C-trap runs fast and shallow because it holds ions rather than filtering them.

cellsPerRadius.description: Grid cells across the inscribed radius. This is the cost knob: the domain is a box around the whole arc, so halving the cell is eight times the nodes.

ejectVolts.description: A steady push across the in-plane pair: the outer rod positive and the inner negative, so a positive ion is driven INWARD, through the slot a real C-trap has in its inner electrode and toward the analyser sitting inside the arc. Zero by default, so the template is a trap unless a document says otherwise - the same way the rectilinear trap carries both of its configurations. A sequence raising this from nought is what an ejection is.

slotHalfTurns.description: Angular width of the slot in the inner electrode, in half turns. This is the hole ions leave through, and without one an ejection pushes the packet straight into metal - which is what this template did before the slot existed, and said so by striking a rod after exactly the inscribed radius of travel. Wider passes more of the packet and weakens the trapping field near it, which is the trade a real design makes.

innerBeads.description: Beads in each of the two inner-electrode segments. Fewer than the other rods because each segment spans less arc.
